title: Trust is designed into the record: Privacy, security, implementation, auditability, and HIM roles
overview: Trustworthy health information systems depend on appropriate access and disclosure, safeguards that protect information and systems, and workflows that are monitored and improved. This week distinguishes privacy from security, examines administrative, physical, and technical safeguards, and applies the Assess → Protect → Monitor → Improve framework to implementation work and HIM responsibilities.
objectives: Explain how privacy and security differ and work together.
Describe how implementation changes workflows and why unanticipated effects must be monitored.
Explain HIM responsibilities in data management, data quality, privacy, security, collection, analysis, and system design.
Use the Assess → Protect → Monitor → Improve framework to organize how trust is supported in a health information system.
Explain how administrative, physical, and technical safeguards support trustworthy systems.

sections.body: Privacy asks who should have access, what may be used or disclosed, and why. Its purpose is to govern appropriate access and disclosure. Security asks how systems prevent, detect, and respond to threats; it protects information and systems. They work together, but they are not interchangeable: a decision about appropriate access is a privacy question, while the controls used to protect systems and respond to threats are security concerns. HIM tools named for privacy include authorization, minimum necessary, policy, and education. Security tools include role-based access, authentication, audit logs, and incident response. Role-based access and audit logs are examples of how controls can support both the practical protection of information and accountable access.
sections.title: Privacy and security: connected responsibilities with different purposes

sections.body: Three safeguard categories organize where controls are applied. Administrative safeguards include policy, training, risk management, and procedures. Physical safeguards concern facilities, devices, media, and environmental controls. Technical safeguards include access, authentication, audit logs, transmission, and integrity controls. These categories describe different kinds of controls rather than competing choices. Trustworthy systems align administrative, physical, and technical safeguards with privacy, security, documentation integrity, and continuous improvement. The quality and safety principles add four design questions: Does the system fit its intended users, work, outputs, and decisions? Is information complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood? Are privacy, security, integrity, and auditability protected? Can people use the information safely and effectively through testing, training, monitoring, and improvement?
sections.title: Safeguards and trustworthy system design

sections.body: Implementation changes workflows, and its effects may not all be anticipated. Therefore, implementation is not complete as a design task alone: workflows need testing, and effects need monitoring so problems can be identified and corrected. In the EHR implementation example, the organization assigns role-based access, trains users, monitors audit logs, reviews incidents, tests workflows, and corrects root causes. Read as a coordinated set of actions, these steps address access, user preparation, evidence from system activity, incidents, workflow performance, and corrective improvement. Monitoring matters because an implementation can alter how work is carried out and create effects that require a response.
sections.title: Implementation requires monitoring and correction

sections.body: HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work. First, explain purpose by identifying users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits. Protect meaning through definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation. Protect quality by checking identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency. Protect trust by supporting privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure. Improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction. The broader HIM role also spans data management, collection, analysis, and system design. Together, these responsibilities keep information fit for its intended use and connect system controls to the work people perform.
sections.title: HIM responsibilities connect purpose, meaning, quality, trust, and workflow

sections.body: The Assess → Protect → Monitor → Improve framework organizes trust work as a continuing sequence. Assess by identifying information, users, risks, and obligations. Protect by applying administrative, physical, and technical controls. Monitor by reviewing access, audit logs, incidents, and data quality. Improve by correcting root causes and improving the system. The stages help organize what happens, who is responsible, and where control is needed. Monitoring provides a basis for identifying issues; improvement then focuses on correcting their root causes rather than treating the stages as isolated activities.

activities.title: Respond to implementation effects
activities.prompt: Hypothetical situation: during an EHR implementation, the organization has assigned role-based access and trained users. It now needs to check whether the changed workflow is producing unanticipated effects. Which action set best follows the implementation example and trust framework?
activities.debrief: Implementation can change workflows and create unanticipated effects that must be monitored. The example includes monitoring audit logs, reviewing incidents, testing workflows, and correcting root causes.
options: Treat training as the final step and stop reviewing workflow or system activity.
Monitor audit logs, review incidents, test workflows, and correct root causes.
Replace monitoring with a general statement of system purpose.
Focus only on data collection and postpone review of access and incidents.
